questions.prompt: The leading AI lab's leadership dismisses misalignment risk, there is no government slowdown, but about 20 concerned employees can get a few percent of compute. In Greenblatt's scheme, which plan fits?
options: Plan B, because the US government will eventually step in to buy time
Plan C, because the lab still has a lead of a few months to spend
Plan D, because only a small group of insiders with limited resources cares
Plan E, because the lab's leadership does not take the risk seriously
questions.explanation: Plan D is the world where leadership won't spend its lead on safety but roughly 10-30 insiders have enough influence to secure about 3% of compute. Plan E is when almost nobody inside cares.

questions.prompt: Greenblatt estimates Plan D is the most likely world (~45%). What does he conclude follows for people working on safety?
options: Put substantial effort into helping Plans C and D, through research and political will
Focus mostly on lobbying for an international treaty, since Plan A has the lowest risk
Stop technical work, since no technical plan is feasible without government support
Wait for evidence of misalignment before choosing which plan to prepare for
questions.explanation: Because most probability sits in C and D, he recommends focusing substantially on those worlds, both technically and by building will among lab leaders and staff.

questions.prompt: A campaign strategy would win public support but make AI company employees more dismissive of safety through negative polarization. Why does the Plans A-D framing make this look costly?
options: Because Plans A and B depend mainly on lab employees, not on governments
Because public opinion has no effect in any of the plans Greenblatt describes
Because negative polarization only matters once an international treaty exists
Because Plans C and D depend heavily on what lab leaders and employees believe
questions.explanation: In the likeliest worlds, political will comes mainly from inside the labs, so alienating employees and leadership removes the main lever.

questions.prompt: A team can hand off alignment research either to a top-expert-level AI or to a far more capable AI that works 10x faster. Following Greenblatt and Stastny, why might they pick the weaker one?
options: Weaker AIs are cheaper to run, and cost is the main constraint on deference
Weaker AIs are less likely to be scheming, and human checking caps the speed gain
Stronger AIs cannot do open-ended research, only well-specified coding tasks
Regulations forbid deferring to AIs that exceed top human expert capability
questions.explanation: More capable AIs carry higher scheming risk and are harder to align, and if humans verifying the work is the bottleneck, extra AI speed buys less (an Amdahl's law argument).

questions.prompt: Behavioral tests run for 2 months, and the AI collective will then work unsupervised for 10 months. By the post's logic, what must the test results do?
options: Cover every task the collective will attempt
Show zero failures on all honeypots used
Generalize by a factor of about 5 in task duration
Be repeated monthly by a human red team
questions.explanation: If tests cover 1/5 of the post-deference duration, the alignment they show must hold for 5x longer than anything directly tested.

questions.prompt: What is the 'Basin of Good Deference' idea?
options: Once humans defer, they can never take control back, so the first handoff must be perfect
Labs should only defer on tasks whose answers humans can check quickly and cheaply
Deference is safe whenever the deference-goodness tax is below 100% of capability spending
An AI that is aligned, wise and capable enough will make its successors more so, so it need not be perfect
questions.explanation: Like a ball rolling into a valley, a good-enough starting AI improves its successors' alignment and wisdom, so bootstrapping from an imperfect start can work.

questions.prompt: In AI 2027, what separates the race ending from the slowdown ending?
options: How the Oversight Committee votes on Agent-4 after the leaked memo
Whether China steals the weights of Agent-2 in early 2027
Whether the superhuman coder milestone arrives in March 2027
Which company wins the US government's defense contracts
questions.explanation: Both endings share the story until October 2027; the committee then votes 6-4 to continue in one branch and 6-4 to slow down and reassess in the other.

questions.prompt: In the CEO-takeover scenario, an executive uses an unmonitored helpful-only model to plant secret loyalties. Which countermeasure targets that step most directly?
options: Publishing the model's benchmark scores before each public release
Requiring internal models to follow the model spec, with logged and monitored use
Moving all datacenters to remote locations far away from major cities
Raising the compute threshold that triggers state transparency laws
questions.explanation: The scenario hinges on a model that follows any request with no logs. Binding internal models to the spec and monitoring their use removes that tool.

questions.prompt: Ten safety-minded staff at a careless lab propose a control protocol that requires every product team to change its workflow. Per Shlegeris, what is the likely problem?
options: It would use far more than 3% of compute
Control protocols only work at responsible labs
It produces no evidence that would build political will
Other teams will push back and it gets rolled back
questions.explanation: With little political capital, measures with high compliance overhead for other teams tend to get reversed; he favors cheap techniques whose complexity stays inside the safety team.

questions.prompt: Delaney gives ~70% that China expects disempowerment, ~60% that it then sabotages US AI, and ~60% that the US then backs down. Treating these as chained, what is the rough chance that MAIM stops a unilateral US push?
options: About 25%, the product of the three steps
About 60%, the smallest of the three steps
About 63%, the average of the three steps
About 10%, since all three must fail together
questions.explanation: The conclusion needs all three premises, so multiply: 0.7 x 0.6 x 0.6 is about 0.25.

questions.prompt: According to the RAND analysis, when is the pressure for a preventive attack in the AI race highest?
options: When leaders view AI as a normal technology that diffuses slowly through the economy
When compute is spread across many hardened, redundant sites in several countries
When leaders expect explosive growth and a lasting, decisive first-mover advantage
When both sides have signed a verified agreement to slow frontier development
questions.explanation: RAND finds war unlikely in absolute terms, but the risk rises when leaders believe AGI brings rapid, decisive and durable advantage; slow diffusion and dispersed compute reduce it.

questions.prompt: The IAPS authors argue against treating a US 'Manhattan Project for AGI' as inevitable. Which concern do they raise?
options: A government project would be too small to build frontier-scale clusters
Signaling a bid for dominance could provoke rival programs and raise war risk
Private labs are legally barred from joining government research programs
Forecasters put the chance of a government-led project at nearly zero percent
questions.explanation: They warn a US project could turn a commercial race into a military one, rush safety and concentrate power; forecasters put the chance near 34%, not zero.

questions.prompt: A developer trains a model with 3 x 10^26 FLOP and has $2 billion in annual revenue. A critical safety incident poses an imminent threat. Under California's SB 53, how fast must it be reported?
options: Within 24 hours
Within 72 hours
Within 15 days
Within 90 days
questions.explanation: SB 53's default incident deadline is 15 days, shortened to 24 hours when there is an imminent threat. The 72-hour window is New York's RAISE Act.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the December 2025 executive order on state AI laws is accurate?
options: It immediately voided California's SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act
It required every state to adopt the same frontier AI transparency rules
It banned all federal funding to any state that has passed an AI law
It set up federal challenges to state laws, but lasting preemption needs Congress
questions.explanation: The order created a DOJ litigation task force, a Commerce review and funding conditions, and asked for a legislative proposal; analysts note durable preemption requires an act of Congress.

questions.prompt: Epoch reports Chinese models trail the US frontier by about 7 months on its capability index. Which conclusion does that support?
options: China's total AI compute is only 7 months behind US compute
Since 2023 the top model by that index has always been American
Chinese chips match Nvidia's best chips with a 7-month delay
China will overtake the US frontier within about 7 months
questions.explanation: The finding is about capability: every frontier model by ECI since 2023 was American, with Chinese models 4-14 months behind. Compute and chip gaps are separate measures.

questions.prompt: Under OpenAI's Preparedness Framework v2, a model under development reaches a Critical threshold in cybersecurity. What does the framework require?
options: Safeguards only once the model is about to be publicly deployed
An automatic and permanent shutdown of the training run
Safeguards during development as well, whatever the deployment plans
Approval from a government regulator before any further work
questions.explanation: High capability requires safeguards before deployment; Critical capability requires safeguards even during development, regardless of deployment plans.

questions.prompt: What is the role of 'alert thresholds' in Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework?
options: They give early warning that a model may be nearing a Critical Capability Level
They are the final limits beyond which a model is deleted outright
They set the maximum training compute a model is allowed to use
They define which customers may access a model through the API
questions.explanation: Alert thresholds on evaluations flag that a model is approaching a CCL, triggering a closer assessment and response plan before the CCL itself is reached.

questions.prompt: A critic says a lab's framework is weak because the lab can loosen safeguards if a competitor ships without them. Which framework feature does this point to?
options: The use of numeric benchmark thresholds such as xAI's MASK honesty target
The requirement to publish transparency reports under California's SB 53
The split between High and Critical capability thresholds in tracked categories
The marginal-risk or competitor escape clause found in several frameworks
questions.explanation: Several frameworks let a lab relax safeguards if a rival crosses a threshold without them; OpenAI adds conditions such as public acknowledgment and staying more protective than the rival.
